title: Lalibela
hook: in Ethiopia, churches carved downward out of solid rock

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gutenberg's Bible, and metal letters that made books cheap. Your line was words for everyone. Did a book change hands? Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

On a plain of reddish stone in the Ethiopian highlands, at first there seems to be nothing to see. Then the ground opens. At the edge of a deep trench, down at the bottom, its roof level with the plain, stands a church. A whole church, with doors and windows and a cross on top, all one piece with the rock around it. Nobody built it up. Somebody dug it down. Pilgrims in white shawls climb down stone steps into the trenches to pray. Today: Lalibela.

Lalibela is a town in northern Ethiopia, named for a king the Ethiopian Orthodox Church honors as a saint. Tradition says King Lalibela wanted a holy city in his own land, a new Jerusalem, for Christians who could not make the long journey to the old one. And so, the tradition goes, churches were cut out of the living rock. Here's how it worked. The carvers started from the top. They cut a trench around a huge block of stone, leaving it standing free. Then they hollowed the block from the inside: rooms, pillars, arches, windows, all carved out, nothing added. If you cut away too much, there was no putting it back. One church is shaped like a cross when seen from above, its roof flat with the ground. The place carries names from the Holy Land. A stream there is called the Jordan. Ethiopian Christianity has its own way. Its church belongs to the family of Oriental Orthodox churches, with its own language of worship, Ge'ez, its own calendar and its own feasts. At Lalibela, crowds of pilgrims gather at Christmas, which Ethiopian Christians call Genna, filling the trenches and the rock-cut courtyards. Isaiah has a line that fits a church dug into stone. In the King James Bible: "look unto the rock whence ye are hewn." And Jesus, in Matthew, says, "upon this rock I will build my church." At Lalibela, that image becomes stone you can touch. The church isn't set on the rock. It is the rock.
screen: `CUT FROM THE TOP, HOLLOWED FROM INSIDE.`
`NOT ON THE ROCK. IT IS THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carve out one hour. The carvers at Lalibela made room by taking away. Look at the week ahead, in your head or on your phone. Find one hour you could cut free, the way they cut a trench around a block of stone. Early in the morning, a lunch break, an evening without a screen. Choose it. Mark it. If you pray, that hour can be for prayer. If you don't, let it be for quiet, a walk, or a long look at something beautiful. The bell holds the time.
Lalibela. A town in Ethiopia, named for a saint-king, where churches were carved down into solid rock as a new Jerusalem.
Your line: churches in the rock. Today, protect the hour you carved out. When something tries to fill it, say no, once, kindly. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Ethiopian Orthodox Christians make pilgrimage to Lalibela, especially at Genna, their Christmas, and at Timkat, the feast of Jesus's baptism, gathering in white shawls in the rock-cut churches to pray and sing.

notes: Claims rule: the outline hook's count ('eleven churches') and any dates are not stated; the new Jerusalem purpose is given as 'tradition says'. Confirm.

Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church as part of the Oriental Orthodox family, Ge'ez as liturgical language, own calendar: confirm.
Genna (Christmas) pilgrimage to Lalibela and Timkat in howItsDone: confirm. Ge'ez spelling ገና for Genna: please verify the script.
Matthew 16:18 is read differently by churches (Peter, Peter's confession, Christ); the script uses it only as an image and does not interpret it. Confirm.
